CMake now requires OpenMP and links it; the executable name is unchanged and no new files or dependencies were added.\n\n**Decomposition design** (all inside the existing `choleskyDecomposition`):\n- The matrix is copied in parallel into contiguous 128×128 tiles, factored, and copied back with the upper triangle zeroed. The row-major layout with power-of-two strides mapped whole tiles onto two L2 sets, which was the first big bottleneck.\n- A 6×8 register-blocked GEMM micro-kernel (GCC vector extensions, AVX2 on this host) works on packed panels. Blocked TRSM and diagonal factorization kernels reuse the same micro-kernel.\n- Each step runs two phases separated by a custom spin barrier. Phase A updates the next block column; the diagonal factorization starts on one thread as soon as that tile's chunks are done. Phase B runs the trailing update on fixed owner threads with work stealing, and the next column's triangular solves are interleaved as soon as the diagonal is ready. Packed panels are double buffered and written with streaming stores.\n- Threads are pinned to distinct CPUs only when no OpenMP binding policy is set, since unbound spinning threads at 256 threads made the OS stack workers on busy cores.\n- Matrix generation and validation loops are also parallelized with identical per-element summation order, so their results are bit-identical to the original.\n\n**Semantics.** Validation passes at every size and thread count tested (1, 7, 128, 256 threads; n from 1 to 8192, including non-multiples of the tile size). The output hash is identical across thread counts, so the result is deterministic. The hash differs from the original binary because the blocked algorithm sums in a different order; relative error is around 1e-9 versus the 1e-6 tolerance. The non-positive-definite path reports the same diagonal index as the original and returns failure.\n\n## Performance\n\nMeasured with 128 threads on a quiet machine earlier in the session. Later runs were 10 to 30% slower because other users' jobs pushed the load average to 50 to 80.\n\n| n | original | new, 128 threads | new, default (256 unbound) |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| 2048 | 2137 ms | 20 ms | 23 ms |\n| 4096 | 17875 ms | 57 ms | 68 ms |\n| 8192 | ~140 s | ~206 ms | ~220 ms |\n\nSingle-thread throughput rose from 1.3 to about 20 GFLOPS.\n\n## Caveats\n\n- Timings on this host are noisy; compare variants back-to-back and take the minimum of several runs.\n- Thread pinning and transparent-huge-page advice are Linux-specific and compiled out elsewhere; streaming stores and the pause instruction are x86-specific with portable fallbacks.\n- Remaining inefficiency is cross-core traffic for panels and C tiles at 128 threads.
